confirmed.description: The ash is missing from Ibrahim's forehead. The bible row for chapter 5 and the script's page 6 cast note say he keeps the ash smear from 5.3 to the end of the chapter. It is there in 5.4, 5.5, 6.2, 6.3, 7.1, 7.4, 8.1 and 8.4, but his forehead is bare in 6.1, so the mark blinks off for one panel.
confirmed.evidence: Page 6, panel 1, Ibrahim seated on the sacks at top left (about x=330, y=290). His face is in clear three-quarter view and the skin between the turban edge and the brows is plain, with no white mark. Checked in a 6x crop.

verdict.reason: The finding holds, but it is minor, not major. On page 6, panel 1, Ibrahim's forehead is bare. He sits at top left on the sacks, about x=460, y=420 in the 1838 px render. A 5x crop shows plain skin between the turban edge and the brows, with no white mark. The rule is written down in three places: bible line 75 ("Ash on his forehead from panel 5.3 to the end of the chapter"), the script's cast note for pages 6-8, and its continuity notes. Nothing in the script or cast overrides makes an exception for 6.1. The absence also shows at print size. In 5.5 his head is smaller than in 6.1, yet the ash still reads there as a clear white smear. Panels 5.4 and 6.3 show it plainly. In 6.2 it is mostly hidden behind the balloon tail. So this is a real one-panel gap. I rate it minor because the mark is meant to be faint, the panel is a busy wide establishing shot, it comes just after a page turn, and the mark is back in the next panels. It is a continuity detail to fix by touching up the existing art, not a costume or identity error that needs a redraw.

confirmed.description: The coastal official's seat and writing kit change partway through the hall scene. In 6.3 and 6.4 he sits cross-legged on a low carved dais with a palm-leaf bundle on his lap, as the script's "slightly raised platform" asks. From 7.4 he is on a tall carved chair with turned finial posts and his legs down. In 8.4 that chair has a caned back, and in 8.3 he works at a carved writing desk with a lidded brass inkwell and a flat sheet. A red conch standard also appears behind him from 7.4 and in 8.1, on the wall that was plain in 6.4.
confirmed.evidence: 6.4: official cross-legged on a low wooden bench, dark plain wall behind. 7.4 (right third of panel): seated upright on a carved chair, one leg down, red banner with silver conch behind. 8.3: brass inkwell and flat sheet on a carved desk, chair post with a ball finial at lower right. 8.4: cane-backed armchair, legs down.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute this. The crops confirm it. In 6.3, 6.4 and 6.5 the official sits cross-legged on a low carved wooden dais, holding a palm-leaf bundle and a stylus, which matches the script's "slightly raised platform" and "palm-leaf records and a stylus". The wall behind him in 6.4 is dark and plain. From 7.4 he sits upright on a tall carved chair with turned finial posts, his mundu hanging down to the floor (legs down), with a red banner bearing a silver conch behind his head. In 7.5 he writes on stacked leaves at a desk with a brass pot. 8.3 is a different setup: a carved writing desk with a flat cream sheet, a lidded brass inkwell, and a chair post with a ball finial at lower right. In 8.4 he leans back in a cane-backed carved armchair with his legs clearly down. The script still calls his seat a "platform" in 7.1, 7.3, 7.4, 8.1 and 8.4, and has him working a palm leaf with a stylus throughout. 8.3 is scripted as "stylus lifted off the leaf", and 7.2 is a deliberate palm-leaf echo of the Chapter 1 ledger. So the paper sheet, inkwell and desk work against an intended motif, and the floor-dais-to-chair switch is visible across consecutive pages of one continuous scene. Nothing in the bible or script allows a chair or desk. The banner is the weakest part of the report. The bible approves a silver conch on red as the Travancore standard, so having one in the hall is fine. Its sudden appearance in 7.4 and 8.1 is minor set inconsistency, even though the 8.1 reverse angle places it oddly. The seat and writing-kit change is a clear but localized set and prop continuity error, which makes it major, not blocker: identity, lettering and story beats are all intact.

confirmed.description: Time of day jumps within the page. The script runs 3.1 late afternoon, 3.2 a darkening sky, then the late light of 3.5. Panels 3.3 and 3.4 are drawn in flat midday light under a clear blue sky, between a sunset panel (3.2) and a golden-hour panel (3.5).
confirmed.evidence: 3.2: sun on the horizon, orange sky. 3.3: bright blue sky with white clouds, hard noon light on Nagoji's face. 3.4: blue sky, neutral daylight on the cart and carter. 3.5: warm amber sky.

verdict.reason:
I looked at full-page and zoomed crops of page 3 and the problem is real. The script's light runs one way down the page: 3.1 late afternoon, 3.2 a darkening sky, 3.5 late light. Page 4 then goes on to dusk in 4.3 and 5.2.

What the panels show:
- 3.1 is warm afternoon light.
- 3.2 has the sun sitting on the horizon under an orange and violet sunset sky.
- 3.3 jumps to a bright, clear blue sky with white cumulus clouds, a sunlit fort and fields, and even daylight on Nagoji's face.
- 3.4 is also flat midday: a blue sky with neutral light on Ibrahim, the cart, the sacks and the carter.
- 3.5 goes back to a warm amber sky.

So the reader goes from sunset to midday and back to golden hour within one page. Panels 3.2 and 3.3 stack directly on top of each other, so the jump shows clearly at print size.

Neither CONTINUITY.md nor the script allows this. The script's light cues are all late afternoon or later. Part of the fault is 3.2, which overshoots "darkening sky" into a full sunset, but 3.3 and 3.4 are wrong whichever way it is read.

The error is confined to two panels' sky and light and does not affect identity, lettering or any story beat. It is therefore major, not a blocker. The fix is to regrade or redraw the backgrounds of 3.3 and 3.4 to the warm late-afternoon light of 3.1 and 3.5, and optionally to soften 3.2 from sunset to a darkening sky.

confirmed.description: A European-style castle stands on the hilltop behind Nagoji: tall crenellated towers and a keep on a rock outcrop. That does not belong on the Travancore paddy and pepper coast, where forts were low laterite walls. It reads as Goa or Europe, and it competes with the pepper-vine beat. The script calls for no fort here.
confirmed.evidence: Upper left of 3.3 (about x 100-260, y 650-710 on the page): a castle with square crenellated towers above tiled-roof houses and coconut palms.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. I cropped page 3, panel 3.3 at full resolution (about x 150-700, y 800-1300 on the 1838x2775 page). A castle in the European style sits on a bare granite hilltop above the tiled-roof houses and palms. It has several tall square towers with crenellations and a central keep, and its silhouette stands out clearly against the sky. At print size it is about half an inch wide, so readers will see it. The script for 3.3 asks only for a close shot of Nagoji, with pepper vines on a support tree at the paddy's edge, and calls for no fort or building on a hill. Neither the script nor CONTINUITY.md allows a fortress here. A hilltop keep with towers like this looks medieval European, not like a Travancore fort of the 1730s with low laterite walls. That makes it a localized setting anachronism, which fits the major definition. It is not a blocker: identity, lettering and the pepper-vine beat are all correct, and the vines on the right still dominate the panel. The fix is cheap: repaint the hilltop as plain jungle or rock, or replace the castle with a low laterite wall.

confirmed.description: Nagoji's left sleeve is rolled up, baring a smooth, unmarked left forearm. The bible and script say that from page 3 the tunic has long sleeves and the left sleeve stays down over the brand. On page 7 the sleeves are down to the wrist in 7.3, where the official's eyeline is meant to rest on that sleeve, then rolled to mid-forearm on both arms in the very next panel, 7.4.
confirmed.evidence: 6.3: Nagoji's left arm (screen right, next to Ibrahim) has the sleeve bunched at the elbow, a bare forearm with no brand, and the bandage only at the wrist. 7.3: sleeves down to the bandaged wrists. 7.4 and 8.4: both cuffs rolled to mid-forearm.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed from zoomed crops. The script's cast block for page 3 onward and panel 3.1 call for a tunic with "long sleeves" and "the left sleeve down over the brand". Panel 7.3 depends on that, since the official's eyeline is meant to "rest on Nagoji's LEFT sleeve, over the brand". The bible's chapter 5 row says nothing about sleeves. The "seen when sleeves are pushed up" wording only starts in the chapter 7-8 row, so nothing in chapter 5 allows rolled sleeves.

What the art shows:
- **6.3:** Both cuffs are rolled to just below the elbow. Both forearms are bare down to the linen wrist wraps. That includes his left arm (screen right, next to Ibrahim), which shows no brand.
- **7.3:** Sleeves are down to the bandaged wrists, as scripted.
- **7.4 (the next panel):** Both cuffs are rolled to mid-forearm again, with bare forearms over his clasped hands.
- **8.4:** The bowing figure has both cuffs rolled, with bare forearms down to the wraps.
- **8.5 (not in the claim):** The upper arm of the sleeping figure also shows a rolled cuff and a bare forearm.

So the sleeves change from 6.2 (down) to 6.3 (rolled) to 7.3 (down) to 7.4 (rolled), and they stay rolled on page 8. Nagoji is large in 6.3, 7.4 and 8.4, so this is easy to see at print size.

The bare left forearm has no brand. In 6.3 and 7.4 that could be put down to the inner forearm facing away from camera. Even so, the sleeve state still breaks the script's instruction, and the panel-to-panel flip is a clear continuity error.

This is a localized costume error, not an identity or missing-beat problem, so it is major, not a blocker.

Side note, outside this claim: the tunic in 6.3 has a buttoned placket. That conflicts with the script's "no buttons, no collar".

confirmed.description: A European-style castle has been painted onto the hilltop behind Nagoji. The script does not call for it, and it does not belong in 1738 Travancore pepper country. Below it are whitewashed villas with red-tiled roofs in a colonial style. Paint the castle out, or replace it with plain wooded hills or a low laterite Kerala wall.
confirmed.evidence: Upper left of the panel, behind Nagoji's head. A sandstone hill-castle with square crenellated towers and battlements sits on a rocky hilltop, and Portuguese-looking tiled villas stand in the trees below. The script asks only for paddy edge and pepper vines on a support tree. Crop: page-03.png around x 150-500, y 890-1250 (full-res px).

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 3, panel 3.3 (crop x 150-560, y 850-1260 of page-03.png). Behind Nagoji's head on the left, a large sandstone castle sits on a bare granite hilltop. It has several square, crenellated towers and a battlemented curtain wall, and it reads as a European or Rajput castle. It is easy to see at print size: it is sharp, it stands against open sky, and it falls on the eye path between Nagoji's face and the first caption. The script asks only for paddy edge and pepper vines on a support tree, nothing like this. CONTINUITY.md requires 1738-1753 Malabar/Travancore with no anachronisms, and a hill castle like this is not a Travancore form: forts there are low laterite walls. It also undercuts Ibrahim's later line "Our fortresses are both. You will see." (5.1) by showing a fortress before the story reaches one. The houses below it are a weaker point: tiled, whitewashed buildings could pass as Kerala houses, so only the castle needs fixing. It is one background element and does not affect identity, lettering or the beat, so this is major, not a blocker. Fix: paint the castle out and leave the wooded hill, or put a low laterite wall in its place.

confirmed.description: Standing rule broken: a lamp with a glass chimney appears in a Kerala setting. The wall-niche lamp on the left gatepost has a clear glass cylinder over its brass bowl. Every other lamp on the page is an open wick, as the rule requires.
confirmed.evidence: Left gate pillar, just above the first guard's spear tip. A brass oil bowl sits on a stone bracket with a translucent glass cylinder over the flame. Full-res area about x 915-1000, y 400-500 on page-06.png. The gate niches in 6.2 are correctly open flames.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 6, panel 1. On the left gate pillar, above the guard's spear tip (about x 915-1000, y 400-500 at full resolution), a brass oil bowl sits on a stone bracket inside a clear glass cylinder. You can see the cylinder's rim, the highlights on the glass and the stone showing through it. It is not a recessed niche. This breaks the CONTINUITY.md standing rule at line 133: Kerala and Travancore lamps are clay or brass with open wicks, with no glass chimneys or glass lanterns. Script 6.1 asks for oil lamps in a Kerala bazaar, so nothing in the script allows it. Every other lamp in the panel is correct: the stall lamps are open brass bowls hanging on chains with bare flames. The lamp is about 7 x 9 mm at print size, but it is one of the brightest things in the panel, right beside the guard's head, so the glass is easy to see. It is a localized anachronism, so the severity is major, not blocker. Fix: repaint it as an open-wick brass or clay lamp with no glass.

confirmed.description: Malayalam lines have no distinct lettering. The script's lettering convention asks for a separate treatment for every (Malayalam) line, and Chapter 4 already set angle brackets <like this> for it. Every Malayalam line in this chapter is lettered as a plain balloon, so the reader cannot tell the Malayalam lines Nagoji cannot follow from the Konkani he can.
confirmed.evidence: 2.2 'Can he travel?' and the healer's 'He should rest another week...' are plain balloons. In 2.3, 'Men like me are paid to be impatient.' (Malayalam, to the healer) and 'Can you ride in a cart, or on a horse?' (Konkani, to Nagoji) look the same. Compare ch04/renders/r12/page-03.png, where every Malayalam balloon is <bracketed>.

verdict.reason:
I'm confirming this one. The art shows it, and the script requires the opposite. The adaptation notes in CHAPTER-05-SCRIPT.md (line 320) say lines tagged (Malayalam) "get a distinct treatment (for example angle brackets)" and that Konkani between Ibrahim and Nagoji is plain. Chapter 4 already uses this convention: on ch04/renders/r12/page-03.png every Malayalam balloon is in <brackets>, and the one Konkani line ("You fought them, yes?") is plain.

In ch05 r2, every Malayalam line is a plain balloon with no brackets, italics or other marking:
- Page 2, panel 2.2: "Can he travel?" and the healer's "He should rest another week..."
- Page 2, panel 2.3: "Men like me are paid to be impatient." (Malayalam) looks the same as "Can you ride in a cart, or on a horse?" (Konkani).
- Page 5, panels 5.2 and 5.3: "Who is he?", "A man who thought he could drown...", and "That one carries storms in his bones." The Malayalam line in 5.3 is followed in 5.4 by Ibrahim's Konkani "I told her you carry horses there too", and both look the same.
- Page 6: the guard's and Ibrahim's lines at the gate (6.1-6.2), "You bring me shipwreck.", "The sea brought him..." and "Name."
- Page 7: "Service?", "You raided them?", "You know their forts?", the two lines about the king, and "What does a Maratha rider know..."
- Page 8: the official's lines as well.

The script's dialogue text carries only the (Malayalam) tag, not literal brackets, and the pipeline lettered the text exactly as written. That is why no brackets appear anywhere in the chapter. Nothing in the bible or the r1-to-r2 review notes waives the convention.

The effect is real: the reader can't tell what Nagoji follows from what he hears only through Ibrahim's translation. This hurts most on pages 2 and 5, where a Malayalam line and Ibrahim's Konkani line sit next to each other.

I rate it major, not blocker. The wording is correct and readable, no beat is missing, and the fix is a relettering pass (add brackets to the tagged lines) with no redraw. It is a chapter-wide inconsistency with Chapter 4, so it is more than polish.

confirmed.description: Same missing Malayalam treatment: the boy's question, Ibrahim's reply and the old woman's line are lettered as plain Konkani-style balloons.
confirmed.evidence: 'Who is he?', 'A man who thought he could drown, then changed his mind.' and 'That one carries storms in his bones.' have no angle brackets, though the script tags all three (Malayalam).

verdict.reason: Confirmed. I zoomed into page 5, panels 5.2 and 5.3. "Who is he?", "A man who thought he could drown, then changed his mind." and "That one carries storms in his bones." use the same plain round white balloon and upright font as the Konkani lines on the same page (5.1, 5.4, 5.5). They have no angle brackets, no italics and no different balloon shape. The script requires a distinct treatment. The Lettering convention note in scripts/CHAPTER-05-SCRIPT.md (line 320) says Konkani is lettered as plain English and "Lines tagged (Malayalam) get a distinct treatment (for example angle brackets)". The script tags all three lines (Malayalam) at lines 171, 173 and 177. This continues the Chapter 4 convention, where angle brackets mark Malayalam that Nagoji cannot follow. Nothing in the bible or the script allows plain lettering here. The exceptions in Chapters 8 and 9 apply only to Padmini and Revathi. As lettered, the reader cannot tell Nagoji does not follow these lines. That flattens the next beat in 5.4, where Ibrahim relays the old woman's remark ("I told her you carry horses there too"). The problem is chapter-wide: the Malayalam lines on page 2 (2.2 and 2.3) are also plain. It is still a localized relettering fix with correct text and no redraw, so major rather than blocker.

confirmed.description: Same missing Malayalam treatment for all the gate and hall dialogue. The only Konkani on the page, Ibrahim's whispers in 6.3, looks the same as everything else, so the language switch the script relies on is lost.
confirmed.evidence: 'You come late, kapitan.', 'This is the man I sent word about.', 'You bring me shipwreck.' and 'Name.' are all plain balloons.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 6. Every Malayalam line uses the same solid white balloon and roman font as the Konkani whispers in 6.3, with no angle brackets, italic tag, tint or border change. That covers "You come late, kapitan." and "The sea does not consult my schedule." in 6.1, the three gate lines in 6.2, "You bring me shipwreck." and Ibrahim's crabs reply in 6.4, and "Name." in 6.5. I zoomed into the 6.1 and 6.3 balloons and they are indistinguishable. The script does not allow this. Its adaptation note (CHAPTER-05-SCRIPT.md, line 320) says lines tagged (Malayalam) get a distinct treatment, for example angle brackets, and that Nagoji hears them only through Ibrahim. Chapter 4 already set the convention by putting Malayalam in <angle brackets> (CHAPTER-04-SCRIPT.md, line 73). The cause is in the script: the ch05 copy lines carry only the "(Malayalam)" speaker tag and no brackets, and the compositor letters copy exactly as written. As rendered, the reader cannot tell that Nagoji does not follow the gate and hall exchanges, so Ibrahim's whispered asides and his translator role on pages 7 and 8 lose their reason. This is major, not a blocker: the words are correct and readable, no redraw is needed, and the fix is to add brackets to the copy and re-letter. The same gap probably affects the other Malayalam lines in the chapter (pages 2, 5, 7 and 8), but this finding is scored for page 6 only.

confirmed.description: Same missing Malayalam treatment, and on this page it changes the meaning. The official's Malayalam questions look the same as Nagoji's direct answers, so Nagoji appears to understand Malayalam unaided. That contradicts Chapter 4 ('I could not follow a word') and the script note that he 'hears them through Ibrahim'.
confirmed.evidence: 7.3: 'You raided them?' / 'Yes.' / 'You know their forts?' / 'Some.' are all plain balloons. The 7.4 and 7.5 official lines ('Our king sharpens his sword...', 'What does a Maratha rider know...') have no brackets.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed on page-07.png at full resolution (crop of 7.3, about x 920-1700, y 700-1280). Every line the official speaks on this page is lettered the same way as Nagoji's: a plain white round balloon in the same font, with no angle brackets, no italic and no tag. The affected lines are "Service?" (7.2), "You raided them?" and "You know their forts?" (7.3), the two "Our king sharpens..." and "He has horse from Madurai..." balloons (7.4), and "What does a Maratha rider know..." (7.5). The source copy is also missing the brackets. In SCRIPT-SNAPSHOT.json these lines are "OFFICIAL (Malayalam)" with plain text. Chapter 4 put the brackets in the copy itself.

Nothing in the script or bible allows plain lettering here. The chapter 5 adaptation notes say lines tagged (Malayalam) "get a distinct treatment (for example angle brackets)", and that Nagoji "hears them through Ibrahim, whose translations are not repeated in balloons." Chapter 4 set the precedent with angle brackets for Malayalam, "which Nagoji cannot follow."

The problem is worst in 7.3. Ibrahim is not in the frame, and "You raided them?" / "Yes." / "You know their forts?" / "Some." reads as a direct two-way conversation in one shared language. That contradicts the chapter 4 POV setup.

Two things keep this at major rather than blocker. The text is correct and every beat lands. Ibrahim is drawn leaning in to Nagoji's ear in 7.4, which hints that he is translating. And the fix is copy only: add brackets to the official's lines and re-letter, with no art redraw. It is still more than a minor cue loss, unlike the missing Marathi tag in chapter 3, because here the missing marker changes what the reader thinks Nagoji can understand.

confirmed.description: Same missing Malayalam treatment on the official's closing lines.
confirmed.evidence: 'You speak well for someone who almost fed the fish.' and 'Tomorrow we take you to the king's war hall...' are plain balloons. The script tags both (Malayalam).

verdict.reason:
Confirmed. In the page 8 crop, panel 8.4 shows both of the official's lines, "You speak well for someone who almost fed the fish." and "Tomorrow we take you to the king's war hall...", in plain white balloons with ordinary text. There are no angle brackets and no other marker. The script tags both lines OFFICIAL (Malayalam). Its lettering note at CHAPTER-05-SCRIPT.md line 320 says Malayalam lines "get a distinct treatment (for example angle brackets)", separate from the Konkani that is lettered as plain English. The bible says nothing that overrides this. The book already uses this convention: ch04 r12 page-03 (printed page 28) letters every Malayalam line inside <...>. On page 8 the official's balloons look exactly like Nagoji's Konkani lines in 8.1 and 8.2, so a reader would think they talk directly and not through Ibrahim, whom 8.1 shows translating.

Cause: the ch05 script tags the speaker but does not put <> around the copy, unlike ch04. SCRIPT-SNAPSHOT.json has 21 lines tagged (Malayalam) and none of them is bracketed, and the compositor letters copy exactly as written. So the same gap also appears on pages 6 and 7 and with the other Malayalam speakers, not just on page 8.

Severity: major, not blocker. The wording is correct and easy to read, and nothing needs redrawing. The fix is to bracket the copy and re-composite the page.

confirmed.description: Nagoji's line 'Who is your king?' is placed on Ibrahim's side of the frame, across his chest just under his hand. The script says to keep all lettering on Nagoji's side so that Ibrahim's wordless flicker reads clearly. The tail points down-left at the caption box's corner, not at Nagoji's head, so the balloon reads as Ibrahim speaking.
confirmed.evidence: The balloon sits at about x 960-1160, y 1590-1675 (display scale) over Ibrahim's vest. Its tail ends near the top-right corner of the caption box (about 895, 1597). Nagoji's head is at the upper left of the panel (about 700, 1350-1550).

verdict.reason: This is real, but it should be minor, not major. The misattribution part of the claim does not hold up. On page 1, panel 1.5, the "Who is your king?" balloon does sit on Ibrahim's side of the frame. It covers his vest and chest below his raised forearm (about 1320-1620 x 2200-2330 at full resolution). But its tail points clearly left and slightly up, away from Ibrahim. It ends next to Nagoji's bare shoulder, just above the top-right corner of the caption box. Following that line leads to Nagoji's figure, not Ibrahim's. The direction is just as clear on a reduced, print-size view of the page. Page 2.1 then gives Ibrahim's evasive answer, which settles who asked. The art also stays readable: the balloon covers none of Ibrahim's face, his gaze, or the thumb on the scar, so the wordless beat still works. What remains true is a small departure from the script, which says to "Keep all lettering on Nagoji's side of the frame." There is plenty of empty wall between the two heads where the balloon could go, with the tail ending nearer Nagoji's mouth instead of stopping at the caption corner. That is polish, not a redraw.

confirmed.description: The opening page grid is ragged, unlike the clean tiers of the approved Chapter 1 page 1. In each two-panel tier the right-hand panel floats lower or shorter than its neighbour, which leaves large empty cream gaps instead of even gutters.
confirmed.evidence: 1.2 runs y 578-1218 but 1.3 runs y 652-1145. 1.4 runs y 1228-1830 but 1.5 runs y 1265-1790. The result is a gap of about 120 px between 1.3 and 1.5 in the right column, where every other gutter is about 8 px. See the downscaled view of page-01.png.

verdict.reason: The problem is real, but it is minor, not major. I measured page-01.png at full 300 DPI resolution (1838x2775) and the reviewer's numbers hold. Panel 1.2 runs y 799-1694 while 1.3 runs y 903-1591, so 1.3 sits about 104 px short at both top and bottom. Panel 1.4 runs y 1699-2542 while 1.5 runs y 1754-2487, about 55 px short each end. That leaves a 163 px gap (about 14 mm in print) between 1.3 and 1.5 in the right column, where the left-column gutter is about 5 px. There is also something the reviewer missed: panel 1.1 spans only x 420-1418 inside a 148-1689 grid, so it is pulled in about 23 mm on each side. The page clearly looks ragged next to the clean tiers of Ch1 page 1, and it shows at print size. The script and the bible say nothing about page geometry, and the fitted layout (LAYOUT-fitted-s3.json, page 1: [104],[214,214],[201.5,201.5]) assumes equal-height tiers. So this is the pipeline's aspect-fit letterboxing (pipeline/layout_fit.py), not a design choice. It is still polish rather than 'clearly wrong': every panel is readable, the reading order works, no action or lettering is cropped or hidden, and no identity or costume is affected. The fix is a re-crop or re-layout (fill the slots or choose another row structure), not a redraw. The pipeline treats letterboxing as a fill penalty, not a failure, and similar inset panels already appear on Ch5 page 2 and Ch4 page 2. Confirmed at minor severity.

confirmed.description: The chapter's establishing 'Wide' is shrunk to a short strip about 65% of the page width. Both captions are set across the middle band of the panel instead of the top, so they bisect the scene: the left box covers the healer's body and the right box covers Ibrahim's torso and the bright doorway reveal.
confirmed.evidence: The panel is only about 720 x 310 px (display scale) at the top of page 1. 'He had decided what kind of man I was...' covers Ibrahim from chest to knee, and 'The man they called kapitan...' covers the healer at the hearth. The thatch and sky band at the top is free for captions, as in ch01 r6 page 1.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed on page 1, panel 1.1 (r2 render, about x 421-1419 and y 359-795 at full resolution). Both caption boxes sit across the middle band of the panel. I compared the render with the raw frame (chapters/ch05/frames/page-01-panel-01-v01.png).

What the boxes hide:
- **Left caption ("The man they called kapitan...").** It covers the whole hearth: the fire, the cooking pot and the healer's body. Only the top of her grey head and one shoulder show. Script 1.1 says she "works at the hearth", and that action is gone from the page.
- **Right caption ("He had decided...").** It runs from about Ibrahim's mid-chest to below his knees. It hides his vest and the scarf, and most of the bright doorway: the palms, sea and boat that make up the script's "backlit by the bright coast" reveal. Its left edge also comes right up against Nagoji's shoulder.

A better position was available. The plaster wall above Nagoji, between the slatted window and the door post, is empty in both the frame and the render. The thatch and sky strip at the top-left is also mostly clear. Nothing in the script, the bible or the review files allows this placement: RESERVE-PIXELS-r2 lists no reserved lines and TEXT-CHECK-r2 only checks the wording.

Severity is major, not blocker. All the lettering is correct and readable, and both figures can still be identified: Ibrahim's turban, beard, mundu and sandals show, and so do the healer's grey hair and sari. But the boxes clearly hide setting and action in the chapter's establishing shot, and moving them should fix it without redrawing anything.

The reviewer's other point, that the panel is only about 65% of the row width, is accurate. The fitted layout gives row 1 a height of 104 and keeps the frame's wide aspect ratio, so the panel narrows. It still reads as a wide shot, so on its own that is minor at most.

confirmed.description: Malayalam lines are not marked as Malayalam anywhere in the chapter. Chapter 4 set the convention of angle brackets <...> for Malayalam that Nagoji cannot follow, and this script's lettering note keeps it. Here every Malayalam line (the boy, the old woman, the gate guard, and all of the official's lines) is lettered exactly like Nagoji's Konkani exchanges. As a result the hall scene reads as if Nagoji understands the official directly, which makes Ibrahim's translating role in 7.4 ('echoing the words low in Konkani') and 8.1 ('leaning in to translate') pointless.
confirmed.evidence: On p6, 'You come late, kapitan.', 'He looks like he should already be dead.', 'You bring me shipwreck.' and 'Name.' are plain balloons. On p7, 'Service?', 'You raided them?' and 'Our king sharpens his sword...' are plain. On p8, 'You speak well...' is plain. Compare ch04 r12 page-03, where Malayalam is lettered '<Kill him. Why bring trouble to the village?>'.

verdict.reason:
I'm confirming this one. The art and the script both bear it out. The script's adaptation notes (CHAPTER-05-SCRIPT.md, line 320) say: "Lines tagged (Malayalam) get a distinct treatment (for example angle brackets). Nagoji hears them through Ibrahim." Chapter 4 r12 page-03 uses that treatment: every Malayalam balloon is wrapped in <...> and the one Konkani line is plain. Chapter 5 r2 has no angle brackets or other marking anywhere. ch05/SCRIPT-SNAPSHOT.json contains no '<' at all. The ch04 snapshot has 14, because the ch04 script wrote the brackets into the dialogue. The ch05 script only tags lines "(Malayalam)", and lettering dropped that tag.

The problem is wider than the reviewer listed. Unmarked Malayalam appears on:
- p2: 2.2 "Can he travel?" and "He should rest another week..."; 2.3 "Men like me are paid to be impatient."
- p5: 5.2 "Who is he?" and "A man who thought he could drown..."; 5.3 "That one carries storms in his bones."
- p6: 6.1 both balloons; 6.2 all three; 6.4 both; 6.5 "Name."
- p7: 7.2 "Service?"; 7.3 "You raided them?" and "You know their forts?"; both 7.4 balloons; 7.5 "What does a Maratha rider know..."
- p8: 8.4 both balloons.

Two things show the harm:
- In 2.3, Ibrahim switches from Malayalam to Konkani ("Can you ride in a cart, or on a horse?") inside one panel, and the switch can't be seen.
- On p6 to p8, Nagoji appears to follow the official directly. That defeats the script's staging of Ibrahim translating ("echoing the words low in Konkani" in 7.4, "leaning in to translate" in 8.1) and breaks the POV convention Chapter 4 set up.

I rate it major, not blocker. The text is correct, and lettering is composited over finished art, so no panel needs redrawing. The fix is to wrap every (Malayalam) line in <...> and re-letter pages 2 and 5 to 8. It does cover the whole chapter, though, so it must be fixed before publication.

confirmed.description: The healer exchange is also lettered without the Malayalam marking, and in 2.3 this changes the meaning. 'Men like me are paid to be impatient' (Malayalam, a reply to the healer) and 'Can you ride in a cart, or on a horse?' (Konkani, to Nagoji) look identical, so both lines read as spoken to Nagoji and the switch between languages is lost.
confirmed.evidence: p2 2.2: 'Can he travel?' and 'He should rest another week...' are plain balloons. p2 2.3: two plain balloons from Ibrahim, one on top of the other, with no angle brackets on the first.

verdict.reason: I confirm this as major. The script and the 300 DPI crop of p2 2.2 and 2.3 both bear it out. The adaptation notes in the Chapter 5 script (scripts/CHAPTER-05-SCRIPT.md, line 320) set the rule: "Lines tagged (Malayalam) get a distinct treatment (for example angle brackets)." Konkani between Ibrahim and Nagoji stays plain. This follows the rule set in Chapter 4, where Malayalam was lettered in <angle brackets>. The script tags these lines as Malayalam: 2.2 "Can he travel?", the healer's reply, and the first line of 2.3, "Men like me are paid to be impatient." The 2.3 follow-up, "Can you ride in a cart, or on a horse?", is untagged, so it is Konkani. In the render, all five balloons in 2.2 and 2.3 have the same plain white shape and stroke, with no brackets, italics or any other marking. In 2.3 the two Ibrahim balloons are stacked and both tails point at him, so nothing on the page shows that he switches from Malayalam to Konkani or that Nagoji cannot follow the healer exchange. That loses a point-of-view beat the script calls for. The reply logic ("Men like you never do" followed by "Men like me...") still lets a reader guess the first 2.3 line answers the healer. The text is correct and readable, so this is not a blocker. It is a real lettering omission against the script's own rule, not a matter of taste, so major fits. The same omission runs through the rest of the chapter: the Malayalam exchanges on page 6 (guard, official) are also plain balloons, so the fix should be applied to the whole chapter, not just page 2.

confirmed.description: This panel contradicts the scene's setting and time of day. A European-style castle with crenellated towers sits on the hill behind Nagoji, which is not in the script and reads as a Portuguese or medieval fort on the Travancore coast. verdict.reason: Confirmed. When I zoom into page 3, panel 3.3, a European medieval castle sits clearly on the hilltop at upper left. It has square crenellated keeps and towers and stands against open sky. It is small, about 130 px wide at 300 DPI, so roughly 0.45 in printed. But it sits in the clear sky of the page's largest panel, so a reader will see it and read it as a European castle. The script (lines 105-109) asks only for a close shot of Nagoji breathing in, with pepper vines on a support tree at the paddy's edge. It calls for no hill fort. Nothing in CONTINUITY.md allows a castle here, and it clashes with the chapter's theme of Kerala forts. The time of day is also wrong. Panel 3.3 is lit like midday, with a saturated blue sky and white cumulus clouds, right after the 3.2 sunset. Panel 3.4 has the same midday light, which makes the jump worse rather than excusing it. This is localized background and lighting work, not an identity, lettering or story-beat failure, so major is the right severity, not blocker.

verdict.reason: Confirmed as major, though the reviewer named the wrong cause. The art is fine and the lettering hides it. The raw frame (/Users/roshanvenugopal/Documents/github/nagoji/output/comic-v15-full-redo/chapters/ch05/frames/page-07-panel-02-v01.png) shows exactly what script 7.2 calls for: the stylus tip resting on the top palm leaf, small incised strokes with no legible script, and the cord and binding hole that mark it as a palm-leaf bundle. On the published page (renders/r2/page-07.png), the frame is cropped tighter. The large off-panel "Huzurat cavalry... netted me." balloon then covers the left third of the panel. That hides the stylus tip, the point where it touches the leaf, the incised marks, and the cord. Mapping the frame onto the render puts the tip and marks at about x 316-368, y 396-417 in the 766x573 panel crop, entirely under that balloon. What a reader actually sees is a hand gripping a stylus over a blank, book-like stack. The tip is never shown touching the leaf, and there are no strokes. So the Chapter 1 ledger echo that 7.1's caption ("written me down as a number") sets up does not come through. Panels 7.4 and 7.5 still show the official with stylus and leaves, so the general idea of writing survives. That is why this is not a blocker. It matches the rubric's "awkward crop hiding the action" (major). The fix is localized and needs no redraw: re-letter 7.2 by moving or shrinking the Nagoji balloon into the empty grey wall at upper left, and loosen the crop so the stylus tip, the marks and the leaf cord stay visible.

refuted.description: Ibrahim's scar is on the wrong side. He faces screen right, so his RIGHT ear and cheek face the camera, and a pale line runs from that RIGHT ear down into his beard. The mark in question doesn't match this chapter's scar. I zoomed in on the original crop (around x 290-350, y 1600-1650) at 7x and 12x. The line is very thin, grey-white, and only about 13 px long (about 1 mm at 300 DPI). It curves roughly level along the top edge of the beard below the cheekbone, in the same tone as the grey flecks in the beard. The real left scar in this chapter looks different. In 7.4 it is a pinkish, straight, hatched line running down from the ear to the jaw, as on the approved sheet's 'LEFT EAR TO JAW SCAR' detail. The 8.4 line is neither pink nor hatched and does not run from ear to jaw, so it reads as grey beard hair or a highlight on the beard edge, not a second scar. refuted.description: Same lighting break on page 4. 4.1 is at sunset and 4.3 to 4.5 move into dusk and blue night, but 4.2 (Ibrahim pulling Nagoji onto the cart) is in bright daylight with a pale blue sky and sunlit palms.

Lower down, the horizon at left glows warm gold (about RGB 174,151,109). Ibrahim's turban, sleeve and the cart are lit by warm light from a low sun. That is the same late golden hour as 4.1. 4.2 is also a different camera direction: a low angle up past Nagoji, where 4.1 looks toward Ibrahim with the sun behind him at right. A bluer sky facing away from the sun is normal at golden hour and does not break continuity. The script gives no time of day for 4.1 or 4.2. The first time it names is 4.3, "Wide. Dusk, the sky shifting...": a later moment further down a broader road, not the same moment at the cart. So the jump from golden 4.2 to dusky 4.3 is the time skip the script asks for, and 4.3 to 4.5 deepen into night as written. 4.2 is a little cooler in the sky than 4.1, but its light is still a low warm sun. At print size that is too slight to read as a lighting error.

refuted.description: The question/answer reading order is unclear. The official's off-panel 'Service?' sits small at the upper right, while Nagoji's large answer balloon fills the left side at almost the same height. A left-to-right reader meets the answer ('Huzurat cavalry...') before the question.
refuted.reason: I refute this one. I measured the panel 7.2 crop at full resolution (x 138-929, y 693-1283 of the 1838x2775 render). The "Service?" balloon runs from crop y 94 to 204. The body of the "Huzurat cavalry..." balloon starts at about y 210 and runs to 555. The two balloons do not overlap in height at all: the question sits entirely above the answer. That is the standard case where the higher balloon is read first, even when it sits to the right. The question's text line (about y 150) is about 150 px (half an inch at 300 DPI) above the first line of the answer (about y 300). The only part of the answer that rises to the question's height is its thin pointer tail, which runs to the top-left corner toward off-panel Nagoji. Pointer tails carry no text and do not set reading order. The natural eye path works: in at the top left, across the empty background to "Service?", then down and left into the answer. The script puts both speakers off-panel (7.2: OFFICIAL (off), NAGOJI (off)), and the art does exactly that. The answer balloon is visually heavy, and "Service?" is a one-word question, so a reader who glances at the big balloon first recovers at once. At most this is optional polish, such as nudging "Service?" a little left or lowering the answer balloon slightly. It is not a major reading-order fault at print size.

refuted.description: The shrine panel loses its key beat. The old woman's eyes are supposed to have already gone past Ibrahim to Nagoji on the cart. Instead she looks straight up into Ibrahim's face while she marks his forehead, so her line 'That one carries storms in his bones' reads as being about Ibrahim. That also breaks the 5.4 payoff, 'I told her you carry horses there too.'
refuted.reason: I'm refuting this one. I cropped page 5, panel 5.3 at full resolution and zoomed in on the old woman's eyes. She is not looking into Ibrahim's face. Ibrahim's eyes are closed, his head is bowed, and his eyes sit at the same height as hers. Her head tilts up and her irises sit high in her eyes, so she is looking up and to the right, above his eyes. I drew a straight line from her eyes to Nagoji's face (upper right, lit by the lantern). It runs just over her marking thumb, through the bottom edge of Ibrahim's turban, and on to Nagoji. Gazing at Ibrahim's brow and gazing past him to Nagoji therefore point the same way in this drawing. If anything, the steep upward look fits looking past him better than looking at him, because looking at his face would need only a level gaze. The art does not show her eyes fixed on Ibrahim. The lettering also supports the script: "That one" is not how she would refer to the man she is touching, and 5.4's "I told her you carry horses there too" confirms she meant Nagoji. Her face is only about 0.2 inch wide at print size, so the eye direction alone cannot be read as a definite mistake. At most, a clearer eyeline to Nagoji would be optional polish. The 5.3/5.4 beat is not broken.

minors.evidence: Official seated on the far platform, center right of the panel. A small red dot is visible between his brows. Full-res area about x 1200-1260, y 1440-1500 on page-06.png. 6.5 shows a clean forehead.

minors.description: The chapter's payoff line is set in a very narrow capsule balloon with 2-3 words per line over ten lines, jammed against the panel's right border. It reads choppily for the climactic statement.
minors.evidence: The 'I know what a horse can do to a musket line when the man in the saddle has stopped being impressed by white skin.' balloon is about 210 px wide in a roughly 550 px panel.

minors.description: Three large balloons take up more than half the frame. They cover the seated men turned toward Nagoji and most of Ibrahim leaning in to translate, the staging the script sets up, even though the rafters and lamps above were meant to hold the lettering.
minors.evidence: 'I know how men like them think...' covers Ibrahim's body and the lower right of the hall. 'Your king knows his own land...' covers the seated men at left centre.

minors.description: The old woman's balloon sits over Ibrahim's chest, and its short tail ends at her forearm rather than her face, so the line can be misread as Ibrahim's.
minors.evidence: 'That one carries storms in his bones.' sits at about x 890-1150, y 760-880 (display scale) on Ibrahim's body. The tail tip is at about (850, 780) on the woman's arm and ash bowl.

minors.description: Ibrahim's opening balloon is a tall, skinny oval with one or two words per line, which is awkward to read next to the normally proportioned answer balloon.
minors.evidence: 'You were on the Portuguese ship. The storm did not like her.' is broken over six lines ('You were on / the / Portuguese / ship. The / storm did / not like her.').

minors.description: The top panel border crops the top of Ibrahim's turban, his main identity tag in two-shots, so his head butts the frame line.
minors.evidence: 2.1: the turban is cut off at the top edge. The same tight crop appears on the turban in 4.4 and on the ash-marked turban in 5.4.

minors.description: Lines the script marks for a quieter delivery are lettered as ordinary full-size solid balloons: 6.3's '(whisper)' and 4.3's '(small)'.
minors.evidence: 6.3 'This is not the king. He is busy elsewhere.' and 'This is one of his hands on this coast.' are standard solid balloons. 4.3 'Rest. The road is long, and the bulls do not hurry.' is full size.

minors.description: The script asks for all lettering to stay on Nagoji's side of the frame so that Ibrahim's wordless flicker reads clean. Nagoji's 'Who is your king?' balloon sits on Ibrahim's half, over his chest and arm. Also, the bright doorway and sea that his gaze should slide toward are not shown, only a blank mud wall.
minors.evidence: p1 panel 5: the balloon spans roughly x 960-1160, y 1590-1680 (display px), on the right half beside Ibrahim's hand-to-jaw pose, while Nagoji occupies the left edge. The background behind Ibrahim's eyeline is plain wall.

minors.description: The silent memory panel does not repeat Chapter 1, 6.5 as specified, which calls for a black mare on a cold winter morning. It shows the mare against a warm golden sunrise over a palm-lined river with a hilltop fort, which reads as the Kerala coast rather than the remembered Deccan. The mare also has a small white forehead star, but the Kanka sheet shows her solid black.
minors.evidence: p2 panel 4 crop: palms, a sun disc and a hill fort at the left, in warm peach and gold tones. Ch1 r6 page-06 panel 5 is grey-blue and misty. Zoom on the mare's forehead shows a white streak between the eyes, which is not on 19-kanka-v15.png.

minors.description: Two misses here. Ibrahim's 'lips twitching toward a smile he does not allow' is drawn as a flat scowl. The top of his turban is also cropped off by the panel border.
minors.evidence: p2 panel 1: the turban crown is cut at the top frame line. His brows are drawn down, his mouth is set and there is no hint of a smile.

minors.description: There is an unscripted white church with a belfry and a red roof on the waterfront in the background. On a road the heroes are taking away from the Portuguese, it reads as a Portuguese colonial church and is a distracting cue.
minors.evidence: Crop of p3 panel 4 background: a white building with a small bell tower and a red-tiled roof on the shoreline, just right of centre behind the cart.

minors.description: Ibrahim's two lines are scripted as whispers, but they are lettered as ordinary full-voice balloons, with no dashed outline or reduced type.
minors.evidence: p6 panel 3: 'This is not the king. He is busy elsewhere.' and 'This is one of his hands on this coast.' have the same solid outline and type size as normal dialogue.

minors.description: The script places the official 'on his platform'. On page 6 he sits cross-legged on a low dais, but here he sits on a cane-backed chair with his legs down, and 7.4 and 8.3 also show a carved chair. His seating changes partway through the scene.
minors.evidence: p8 panel 4: the official sits upright in a chair with a woven cane back and armrests, feet down. On p6, panels 6.3 and 6.4, he is cross-legged on a raised wooden dais.
